summary: Specifies the data export format for version 9 of Cisco's NetFlow services, used by network elements and matching collectors. It uses templates, which describe collections of fields, to make observations of IP packet flows flexible and extensible.

plainLanguage.summary: A router sends a report about the traffic it saw. The report has a header listing what each column means, so it can carry whatever columns are needed.

questions: how does netflow version 9 differ from earlier versions
subtitle: How a router describes its traffic reports with templates so the format can grow without a new version.

tldr.problem: Earlier NetFlow versions had a fixed record layout, so adding one new field meant a new export protocol version and a new collector that could parse it.
tldr.mechanism: Version 9 sends template records that describe which fields, with which lengths, the following data records contain. Export packets are a small header followed by template, options template and data FlowSets.
tldr.outcome: Collectors can decode records without knowing every field's meaning. The IPFIX working group took NetFlow version 9 as the basis of its new protocol.

today: RFC 3954 is an Informational RFC with no obsoleting or updating RFC in the metadata, and it states that it documents the protocol as submitted to the IETF as a basis for IPFIX work. See RFC 3917 for the IPFIX requirements and RFC 3955 for the evaluation that recommended it as the basis.

sections.title: Template-Based Flow Export
sections.content:
Cisco Systems' NetFlow services let network elements such as routers and switches gather IP flow information and export it to collectors. A flow is a unidirectional sequence of packets with common properties that pass through a network device. Records include IP addresses, packet and byte counts, timestamps, type of service, ports and interfaces.

Version 9 uses templates. A template defines a collection of fields with descriptions of their structure and semantics. This lets new fields be added without changing the record format, lets a collector interpret a record even if it does not understand a new field, and lets an exporter send only the fields needed, reducing data volume.

The IESG note says this RFC documents the protocol as it was when submitted to the IETF as a basis for IPFIX work. It is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard and did not have complete IETF review for security or congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: Old reports had fixed columns. Version 9 sends a legend first that says what the columns are, so new columns can be added any time.

sections.title: Exporters, Collectors and FlowSets
sections.content:
An Exporter is a device with NetFlow services enabled that creates flows from observed packets. A Collector receives flow records from one or more Exporters. An Observation Domain is the largest aggregatable set of observation points at the device, for example a router line card.

An Export Packet is a Packet Header followed by one or more FlowSets. A FlowSet is a collection of records with a similar structure, and there are three kinds: Template FlowSet, Options Template FlowSet and Data FlowSet. A Template Record defines the layout of a Flow Data Record, and an Options Template Record defines an Options Data Record. All binary integers MUST be in network byte order.

Export Packets are normally sent in UDP datagrams, but version 9 is designed to be transport independent and can run over congestion-aware protocols such as SCTP. Because UDP is not congestion aware, the RFC advises a dedicated link between Exporter and Collector, or an export path that can sustain the maximum burstiness.
sections.plainLanguage: The router is the sender and the collector is the receiver. Each parcel has a label on top and then boxes inside: legend boxes and data boxes.

sections.title: The Export Packet Header
sections.content:
The Packet Header has five fields. Version is 9. Count is the total number of records in the packet: Options, Template and Data FlowSet records added together. sysUpTime is milliseconds since the device first booted, and UNIX Secs is the time in seconds since 0000 UTC 1970 at which the packet left the Exporter.

Sequence Number is a cumulative counter of Export Packets sent from the current Observation Domain; Collectors SHOULD use it to find out whether packets were missed. Source ID is a 32-bit value identifying the Observation Domain, and Collectors SHOULD combine the source IP address with the Source ID to separate export streams from the same Exporter.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on the parcel says which version it is, how many items it holds, when it was sent, its place in the series, and which part of the router it came from.

sections.title: Templates, Data and Options
sections.content:
A Template FlowSet has FlowSet ID 0 and holds one or more Template Records. Each record has a Template ID, a Field Count, and then a Field Type and Field Length for each field. Template IDs for data start at 256; values 0 to 255 are reserved. Field types are numbered, for example IN_BYTES is 1, IN_PKTS is 2, IPV4_SRC_ADDR is 8 and IPV4_DST_ADDR is 12. Some types have a variable length N, such as 4 bytes by default for byte counters, so a core router can use 8 bytes where an access router needs only 4.

A Data FlowSet uses the Template ID as its FlowSet ID, then carries records laid out as the template said. The Exporter SHOULD pad so the next FlowSet starts on a 4-byte boundary, and the Length includes the padding.

Options carry information about the NetFlow process itself rather than about flows, for example a sampling rate. An Options Template FlowSet has FlowSet ID 1 and adds scope fields, whose types are 1 System, 2 Interface, 3 Line Card, 4 Cache and 5 Template.
sections.plainLanguage: The legend box says: first column is the sender, second is the receiver, third is the number of packets. The data boxes then hold only the numbers, in that order.

sections.title: Template Management and the Collector
sections.content:
Since the template is not in every packet, the Collector MUST store it to decode later data. Template IDs are unique only within an Observation Domain, and they are lost if the Exporter or NetFlow process restarts. If a Collector gets a new definition for an existing Template ID, it MUST discard the old one.

After a restart, the Exporter MUST NOT send a Data FlowSet without sending the matching template in an earlier packet or the same packet. After configuration changes it SHOULD send new templates at an accelerated rate. It MUST also resend all templates regularly, either every N Export Packets or every N minutes, and both MUST be configurable. This is because templates have a limited lifetime at the Collector.

A Collector SHOULD hold records until their template arrives, MUST NOT decode records with an expired template, and MUST accept padding. It must not assume the template and its data are in the same packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The router repeats the legend every so often, in case the receiver lost it. The receiver keeps the legend and throws away old ones when a new one arrives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NetFlow version 9 was designed expecting the Exporter and Collector to stay within a single private network. The designers imposed no confidentiality, integrity or authentication requirements because these reduced efficiency. If the protocol is used over the public Internet, an attacker might capture, modify or insert Export Packets.

Export Packets are not encrypted, so observers can learn about active flows, endpoints and traffic patterns. Flow records could be forged, and forged templates could leave a Collector unable to decode packets. Denial of service against the Collector is not addressed by the protocol. The RFC says the IPFIX protocol, which uses NetFlow version 9 as its base, addresses these issues, and points to RFC 3917 for its security discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports were made for a private network, so they are not locked or signed. On the open Internet a snoop could read them or slip in fake ones.

fields.name: Version Number
fields.desc: Version of the flow record format; 9 for this version.

fields.name: Count
fields.desc: Total records in the packet: options, template and data.

fields.name: sysUpTime
fields.desc: Milliseconds since the device first booted.

fields.name: UNIX Secs
fields.desc: Seconds since 0000 UTC 1970 when the packet left the Exporter.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Cumulative counter of Export Packets from the Observation Domain.

items.desc: FlowSet ID equals the Template ID of the template that describes it.
